title: The weaker brother (1 Corinthians 8)
hookLine: knowledge puffs up, love builds up
tomorrow: how can one man be 'all things to all men' and stay himself?

lines: WIN THE ARGUMENT, LOSE THE FRIEND.
cards: Win the argument, lose the friend: it happens at plenty of dinner tables. Corinth's next question is about dinner. Some meat in the city had been "offered unto idols."
Can a believer eat it? One group has the answer ready: an idol is nothing, there's one God, meat is meat. Paul agrees with them on the facts.
Then he says the facts aren't the end of it.

teach.b: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth." Charity, in the King James, is love.
Knowledge inflates; love builds. Paul grants the theology: "we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one." But not everyone feels it in their bones.
Someone who used to honor those idols sees a fellow believer eating in an idol's temple, and their tender conscience is pulled back toward what they left.
So: "take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak."
Then the line that names the day: "And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?" The weaker brother isn't a problem to fix. He's someone Christ died for.
And Paul's own choice is blunt: "if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth".
The whole week ran this way: a trembling man, a planter who isn't the point, fools who bless. Being right is half the question. The other half is what my freedom does to the person next to me.

how: Christians turn to 1 Corinthians 8 when they think about freedom and conscience; some churches apply it to choices like drinking around someone who is struggling, and Christians weigh those choices differently.

o: a believer whose conscience is still tender
a younger brother who inherits less land
a disciple who ran away at the arrest

games.q: the week inside one letter — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says the confident group is wrong about idols
he agrees an idol is nothing. his point is love, not facts.
in the King James, charity here means love
knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Paul says the weaker brother should just toughen up
he's someone Christ died for; Paul would rather eat no flesh.

games.q: your friend's family doesn't game on Sundays; your family does. he's at your house on a Sunday. what does 1 Corinthians 8 suggest?
o: pick something else to do, so his conscience isn't pushed.
play anyway; his family's rule isn't binding on you.
explain to him why his family's rule makes no sense.
games.why: Paul grants the facts, then sets his freedom aside for the one whose conscience is tender: love builds up.

practice: Bring to mind one freedom you have that someone near you struggles with: a drink, a kind of joke, a way of spending.
Name the moment it might come up this week, and decide now what you'd set aside for them, quietly, without a speech.

wordCard.voice: The weaker brother. The one whose conscience is still tender, and who, Paul says, is someone Christ died for.

orig.note: Greek: but love builds up. the KJV has but charity edifieth.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: love builds up, even when you're right and the facts are on your side. That's the week.
